title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 10.4.1 Writing: Creative Writing (Descriptive Compositions)

PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A descriptive composition paints a picture with words. In this sub-strand you will name the parts of a description, organise ideas into clear paragraphs, and write a composition of about 80 to 100 words on personal hygiene or keeping a place clean. You will also proofread your work before you display it.

## Strand 10.0: Hygiene and Sanitation
Sub-strand 10.4.1: Writing: Creative Writing (Descriptive Compositions)
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) describe the parts of a descriptive composition for self-expression
b) organise thoughts clearly, precisely and creatively into a coherent paragraph for self- expression
c) create a descriptive composition of about 80-100 words on various topics for effective communication
d) promote the role of creativity in descriptive writing for effective communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Descriptive Compositions

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should you organise your thoughts in clear sentences and paragraphs?
2. How can you tell others about yourself?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: This is achieved as the learner writes descriptive compositions for effective communication.
• Learning to learn: It is enhanced as the learner works with peers to discover how to write descriptive compositions.

## Values
• Responsibility: This is nurtured as the learner engages in assigned roles and duties in different activities of planning and writing a descriptive composition.
• Unity: It is achieved as the learner shares the available resources like the digital devices so that peers can as well type their descriptive compositions on the device.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Proper Sanitation: This is achieved as the learner talks about ‘how to clean a house’ before peers making them learn sanitation from each other.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner relates the skill of descriptive writing to writing skills taught in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 10.0 Hygiene and Sanitation, Sub-strand 10.4.1 Creative Writing: Descriptive Compositions

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Parts of a descriptive composition

LESSON 1: PARTS OF A DESCRIPTIVE COMPOSITION
============================================

## What you will learn
• Name the parts of a descriptive composition.
• Find the paragraphs in a sample of about 80 to 100 words.
• Notice the describing words that build a picture.

Curriculum outcomes: a) describe the parts of a descriptive composition for self-expression

## Introduction
If you tell a friend only 'We cleaned the house', the friend learns the fact but cannot picture the morning. A description adds what you saw, heard, smelled and felt, in an order a reader can follow.

## Notes
### The parts
A descriptive composition has four parts.

- A title that names the topic.
- An opening that tells the reader what is being described and sets the scene.
- A middle, usually one or two paragraphs, that gives details in a clear order.
- A closing that leaves a final picture or a feeling.

Each paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea. You can see a new paragraph because the first line starts a little way in from the margin, or because there is a blank line before it.

### A sample to read with a partner
**Saturday Cleaning**

Our house smells fresh on Saturday morning. I open the windows so cool air moves through the rooms. My brother sweeps with a soft broom while I wipe the table and chairs. Dust rises in the light, then settles in the dustpan.

In the kitchen, Mother scrubs the pots until they shine. I rinse the cups and set them on a clean tray. We empty the bin and wash our hands with soap.

By noon the floor is dry, the windows are clear and the rooms look tidy. I feel proud because we all helped.

That sample has a title and three paragraphs. The first paragraph describes the rooms. The second describes the kitchen. The third closes with the result and a feeling. It has about 95 words, inside the 80 to 100 range.

### What makes it descriptive
The writer does not only name actions. The writer shows them: cool air, a soft broom, dust in the light, pots that shine, a clean tray. Verbs are precise: open, sweeps, wipe, scrubs, rinse, empty. Adjectives such as fresh, soft, clean and tidy help the reader see the house.

The order is easy to follow: morning, then the kitchen, then noon. A reader who can follow the order can picture the work.

## Key words
• descriptive composition — a piece of writing that paints a picture of a person, place or activity
• paragraph — a group of sentences about one main idea
• adjective — a word that describes a noun, such as soft or tidy

## Worked examples

### Example 1
How many paragraphs does Saturday Cleaning have, and what is each one about?

Working:
1. Count the blocks of text under the title.
2. Say the main idea of each block.

Answer: Three. The rooms in the morning, the kitchen work, and the tidy house at noon with the writer's feeling.

### Example 2
Find two describing details in the first paragraph.

Working:
1. Look for words that help you see, feel or smell something.

Answer: Any two, for example: the house smells fresh; cool air; a soft broom; dust in the light.

## Activity: Mark the paragraphs
You will need: A copy of Saturday Cleaning, Coloured pencils
1. Read the sample aloud with a partner, one paragraph each, then the closing together.
2. Draw a box around the title, the opening paragraph, the middle paragraph and the closing paragraph.
3. Underline four words or phrases that help you picture the cleaning.
4. Tell your partner which paragraph was easiest to imagine, and why.

## Practice
1. Name the four parts of a descriptive composition.
2. What is a paragraph?
3. Why does the sample end with a feeling?
4. Replace the dull verb in this sentence with a more precise one: I did the pots until they were clean.

## Summary
• A description needs a title, an opening, a detailed middle and a closing.
• Each paragraph deals with one idea.
• Precise verbs and adjectives help the reader picture the scene.

### Answers to practice
1. Title, opening, middle (details) and closing.
2. A group of sentences about one main idea.
3. The closing leaves the reader with a final picture and shows what the cleaning meant to the writer.
4. Example: I scrubbed the pots until they shone.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: One clear paragraph

LESSON 2: ONE CLEAR PARAGRAPH
=============================

## What you will learn
• Order ideas before writing.
• Write a coherent paragraph with a topic sentence and details.
• Write four descriptive sentences on personal hygiene.

Curriculum outcomes: b) organise thoughts clearly, precisely and creatively into a coherent paragraph for self- expression

## Introduction
A paragraph falls apart when every sentence jumps to a new topic. If you plan the order first, the reader can walk through your idea from the first sentence to the last.

## Notes
### Before you write
Think, then write. Choose one small topic, such as how you wash your hands or how you clean your shoes. List four details. Put them in an order that makes sense: first, next, then, last. Leave out anything that belongs to a different topic.

### The shape of a paragraph
A coherent paragraph holds together.

- The topic sentence tells the reader the one idea.
- The next sentences add details, often in time order or from the largest thing to the smallest.
- The sentences link. Words such as first, then, after that and finally show the order.
- The last sentence can close the idea without starting a new one.

Here is a plan about washing hands.

Topic: washing hands before a meal.
Order: wet, soap, scrub, rinse.
Leave out: what I ate afterwards. That is a new topic.

### A paragraph from the plan
I wash my hands carefully before I eat. First I wet them under clean running water. Then I rub soap over the palms, the backs and between the fingers. After that I scrub under my nails and rinse until the soap is gone. My hands feel cool and clean, ready to touch food.

Every sentence stays on handwashing. The reader can act out the steps.

### Four descriptive sentences
You can also write four separate descriptive sentences on one hygiene topic. Each sentence should show a detail, not only name it.

- The white soap grows slippery and small in my wet hands.
- Bubbles gather between my fingers like tiny glass beads.
- I scrub the nails where dark lines of dust hide.
- Clean water carries the foam away and leaves my skin fresh.

Those four sentences could later become the middle of a composition. Precise pictures make the writing creative without leaving the topic.

## Key words
• coherent — clear and connected, so the parts fit together
• topic sentence — the sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph
• detail — a small piece of information that makes a picture clearer

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Which sentence does not belong? I rinse the cup. I dry it with a clean cloth. Football practice is on Friday. I place the cup on the tray.

Working:
1. The topic is washing a cup.
2. Find the sentence about a different topic.

Answer: Football practice is on Friday.

### Example 2
Write a topic sentence for a paragraph about sweeping your room.

Working:
1. Name the one idea the paragraph will explain.
2. Keep it general enough for details to follow.

Answer: Example: I sweep my room every morning before I leave for school.

## Activity: Four sentences on personal hygiene
You will need: Exercise book, Pencil
1. In pairs, talk about one hygiene activity you both do, such as washing your face, cleaning a handkerchief or scrubbing your shoes.
2. Agree on four details and put them in order.
3. Each learner writes four descriptive sentences. Do not copy your partner's words.
4. Read the sentences aloud and check that every sentence stays on the same topic.

## Practice
1. What does a topic sentence do?
2. Put these details in a sensible order: rinse the soap off; wet the hands; scrub with soap; dry the hands.
3. Add a linking word and rewrite: I dust the window sill. I shake the cloth outside.
4. Write one descriptive sentence about a broom.

## Summary
• Plan the details and their order before you write.
• A paragraph needs one topic sentence and details that stay on that topic.
• Linking words such as first, then and after that keep the paragraph coherent.

### Answers to practice
1. It tells the reader the one main idea of the paragraph.
2. Wet the hands; scrub with soap; rinse the soap off; dry the hands.
3. Example: I dust the window sill. Then I shake the cloth outside.
4. Example: The broom's stiff bristles push a grey line of dust across the floor.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Writing and proofreading a short description

LESSON 3: WRITING AND PROOFREADING A SHORT DESCRIPTION
======================================================

## What you will learn
• Write a descriptive composition of about 80 to 100 words in two or three paragraphs.
• Proofread spelling, capital letters and full stops.
• Explain how creativity makes descriptive writing stronger.

Curriculum outcomes: c) create a descriptive composition of about 80-100 words on various topics for effective communication; d) promote the role of creativity in descriptive writing for effective communication

## Introduction
You already know the parts and how to build one paragraph. Now you put them together into a full composition about cleaning, then you check it before anyone else reads it.

## Notes
### Choose a topic and plan
Good topics for this length are small enough to finish: how we clean our house, how I prepare for school in the morning, or how our class cleans the compound. A plan for 'How we clean our house' might look like this.

- Paragraph 1: the rooms, sweeping and dusting.
- Paragraph 2: the kitchen and the bin.
- Paragraph 3: how the house looks and how I feel.

Aim for about 80 to 100 words. That is two or three short paragraphs, not a long story. If you pass 100 words, cut a sentence that repeats an idea. If you are under 80, add one picture detail.

### Write with creativity
Creativity here means choosing your own true details and fresh words. Do not copy the sample from the first lesson. If your family mops before sweeping, write that. If the soap smells of lemon, say so. A reader enjoys a detail that could only come from you.

Creativity still has to be clear. A surprising comparison is useful when it helps the picture: 'The wet floor shone like a quiet river.' It is not useful if the reader cannot tell what you mean.

### Proofread
Read the composition twice.

- Once for meaning: Does each paragraph have one idea? Is the order clear? Are there about 80 to 100 words?
- Once for mistakes: capital letters for the title and sentence starts, full stops or question marks at the ends, and spelling of words such as soap, sweep, rinse, because and clean.

Change anything that is wrong. Then write a neat copy or type it, and display it where the class can read it. Displaying your work shows that you are willing to share a piece you have checked.

Creative descriptive writing matters because it lets other people see what you see. A tidy composition about a clean house can teach a reader your routine and your care at the same time.

## Key words
• proofread — to read your own writing carefully and correct mistakes
• creativity — using your own ideas and fresh details in a clear way
• composition — a piece of writing made of planned paragraphs

## Worked examples

### Example 1
This closing is dull: 'That is the end of my composition.' Replace it with a descriptive closing about a clean kitchen.

Working:
1. Show the kitchen, or say how you feel.
2. Do not announce that the writing has ended.

Answer: Example: The pots shine, the cups stand in a row and the kitchen smells of soap.

### Example 2
Proofread: yesterday i sweeped the floor and rinse the cups

Working:
1. Capital letter and full stop.
2. Yesterday needs the past tense: swept, rinsed.

Answer: Yesterday I swept the floor and rinsed the cups.

## Activity: Write, check and display
You will need: Exercise book, A digital device to share, if available, A space to display work
1. In pairs, talk about how you clean your house. Each learner notes four details.
2. Write a descriptive composition of about 80 to 100 words in two or three paragraphs.
3. Proofread with the checklist: meaning, order, word count, capital letters, full stops and spelling.
4. Write a neat copy or type it, then display it for the class to read.

## Practice
1. How long should this descriptive composition be, and how many paragraphs should it have?
2. Name two things you check when you proofread.
3. Why is creativity useful in a description?
4. Write a title and a topic sentence for a composition about cleaning your shoes.

## Summary
• Plan two or three paragraphs and write about 80 to 100 words.
• Use your own details so the description is creative and clear.
• Proofread, then display or type the neat copy.

### Answers to practice
1. About 80 to 100 words, in two or three paragraphs.
2. Any two: meaning, order, word count, capital letters, full stops, spelling.
3. Your own details and fresh words help the reader picture the scene clearly.
4. Example title: My School Shoes. Topic sentence: Every Sunday I clean my school shoes until they look neat again.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 10.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (DESCRIPTIVE COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which set names the parts of a descriptive composition?
   A. Title, poem, chorus
   B. Title, opening, middle, closing
   C. Question, answer, mark
   D. Date, greeting, signature only

2. What is a paragraph?
   A. A single adjective
   B. A group of sentences about one idea
   C. The title of a composition
   D. A spelling mistake

3. In the sample Saturday Cleaning, the second paragraph is mainly about
   A. the kitchen
   B. a football match
   C. the school bus
   D. a rainy night

4. Which sentence best works as a topic sentence?
   A. Then the soap.
   B. I clean my handkerchief every evening.
   C. Because.
   D. And the water.

5. Which sentence does not belong in a paragraph about sweeping a room?
   A. I push the broom under the bed.
   B. Dust gathers in the dustpan.
   C. The river is full of fish.
   D. I shake the broom outside.

6. Which linking words help time order in a paragraph?
   A. first, then, finally
   B. or, nor, yet
   C. under, behind, beside
   D. wow, oh, hey

7. About how long should the composition be?
   A. 10 to 20 words
   B. 80 to 100 words
   C. 800 words
   D. one word

8. How many paragraphs should that composition have?
   A. Ten
   B. One word only
   C. Two or three
   D. No paragraphs

9. Why should you proofread before you display your work?

10. What does creativity add to descriptive writing?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 10.4.1 WRITING: CREATIVE WRITING (DESCRIPTIVE COMPOSITIONS)
========================================

1. B. Title, opening, middle, closing
   A description has a title, an opening, a detailed middle and a closing.

2. B. A group of sentences about one idea
   The sentences in a paragraph belong to the same main idea.

3. A. the kitchen
   The second paragraph describes scrubbing pots, rinsing cups and emptying the bin.

4. B. I clean my handkerchief every evening.
   A topic sentence states the main idea in a complete sentence.

5. C. The river is full of fish.
   A sentence about fish leaves the topic of sweeping.

6. A. first, then, finally
   First, then and finally show the order of actions.

7. B. 80 to 100 words
   The task is a short composition of about 80 to 100 words.

8. C. Two or three
   Two or three coherent paragraphs fit 80 to 100 words.

9. So that meaning, order, capital letters, full stops and spelling are correct for the reader.
   Proofreading catches mistakes before other people read the piece.

10. Your own true details and fresh words, so the reader can picture the scene clearly.
   Creativity makes the picture vivid while the writing stays clear.

Answer: Yesterday I swept the floor and rinsed the cups.

## Activity: Write, check and display
You will need: Exercise book, A digital device to share, if available, A space to display work
1. In pairs, talk about how you clean your house. Each learner notes four details.
2. Write a descriptive composition of about 80 to 100 words in two or three paragraphs.
3. Proofread with the checklist: meaning, order, word count, capital letters, full stops and spelling.
4. Write a neat copy or type it, then display it for the class to read.

## Practice
1. How long should this descriptive composition be, and how many paragraphs should it have?
2. Name two things you check when you proofread.
3. Why is creativity useful in a description?
4. Write a title and a topic sentence for a composition about cleaning your shoes.

## Summary
• Plan two or three paragraphs and write about 80 to 100 words.
• Use your own details so the description is creative and clear.
• Proofread, then display or type the neat copy.

### Answers to practice
1. About 80 to 100 words, in two or three paragraphs.
2. Any two: meaning, order, word count, capital letters, full stops, spelling.
3. Your own details and fresh words help the reader picture the scene clearly.
4. Example title: My School Shoes. Topic sentence: Every Sunday I clean my school shoes until they look neat again.

questions.question: Which set names the parts of a descriptive composition?
questions.explanation: A description has a title, an opening, a detailed middle and a closing.

questions.question: What is a paragraph?
options: A group of sentences about one idea
questions.explanation: The sentences in a paragraph belong to the same main idea.

questions.question: In the sample Saturday Cleaning, the second paragraph is mainly about
questions.explanation: The second paragraph describes scrubbing pots, rinsing cups and emptying the bin.

questions.question: Which sentence best works as a topic sentence?
options: I clean my handkerchief every evening.
questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the main idea in a complete sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence does not belong in a paragraph about sweeping a room?
options: I push the broom under the bed.
The river is full of fish.
questions.explanation: A sentence about fish leaves the topic of sweeping.

questions.question: Which linking words help time order in a paragraph?
questions.explanation: First, then and finally show the order of actions.

questions.question: About how long should the composition be?
questions.explanation: The task is a short composition of about 80 to 100 words.

questions.question: How many paragraphs should that composition have?
questions.explanation: Two or three coherent paragraphs fit 80 to 100 words.

questions.question: Why should you proofread before you display your work?
questions.answer: So that meaning, order, capital letters, full stops and spelling are correct for the reader.
questions.explanation: Proofreading catches mistakes before other people read the piece.

questions.question: What does creativity add to descriptive writing?
questions.answer: Your own true details and fresh words, so the reader can picture the scene clearly.
questions.explanation: Creativity makes the picture vivid while the writing stays clear.
